answer_text:
The displayed integral
\[
\int_{\partial F} v\cdot d\mathbf r
\]
is a **line integral** around the boundary curve of the hemisphere, not a flux integral through the curved surface. Let \(F\) be the upper hemisphere
\[
x^2+y^2+z^2=4,\qquad z\ge 0,
\]
so its boundary is the circle
\[
C=\partial F:\quad x^2+y^2=4,\quad z=0.
\]

Assume the standard orientation induced by the outward normal of the upper hemisphere. This is counterclockwise when viewed from the positive \(z\)-axis.

By Stokes’ theorem,
\[
\int_{\partial F} v\cdot d\mathbf r
=
\iint_F (\nabla\times v)\cdot \mathbf n\,dS.
\]

Compute the curl. Write
\[
v=(P,Q,R)=\left(-x^3-2y,\;3y^5z^6,\;3y^6z^5-z^4\right).
\]
Then
\[
\nabla\times v
=
\begin{vmatrix}
\mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k\\
\partial_x & \partial_y & \partial_z\\
P & Q & R
\end{vmatrix}.
\]

We have
\[
R_y=18y^5z^5,\qquad Q_z=18y^5z^5,
\]
\[
P_z=0,\qquad R_x=0,
\]
\[
Q_x=0,\qquad P_y=-2.
\]
Thus
\[
\nabla\times v=(0,0,2).
\]

Instead of integrating over the curved hemisphere, we may use the flat disk
\[
D=\{(x,y,0):x^2+y^2\le 4\}
\]
with upward normal \(\mathbf n=\mathbf k\), since it has the same boundary \(C\). Then
\[
(\nabla\times v)\cdot \mathbf n = 2.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\int_{\partial F} v\cdot d\mathbf r
=
\iint_D 2\,dA
=
2\cdot \operatorname{Area}(D)
=
2\cdot \pi(2)^2
=
8\pi.
\]

So, with the usual outward-induced orientation,

\[
\boxed{8\pi}
\]

If the boundary were oriented clockwise instead, the value would be \(-8\pi\).
